subject: Archaeology
title: The Kyrenia Ship: Ancient Greek Merchant
description: A micro-lesson that makes The Kyrenia Ship: Ancient Greek Merchant usable.

hook.text: A Greek merchant ship from 300 BCE was found off Cyprus with its cargo of almonds and wine still intact.

buildup.text: The Kyrenia ship was a small coastal trader — 47 feet long, carrying 400 amphorae of wine and 10,000 almonds.

discovery.text: Lead sheathing on the hull protected against shipworms. The Greeks invented anti-fouling technology 2,300 years ago.

twist.text: The ship shows signs of pirate attack: spearheads embedded in the hull and cargo scattered as if searched.

climax.text: A full-size sailing replica was built and crossed the Mediterranean, proving the original design was fully seaworthy.

punchline.text: Pirates sank a wine ship. The sea aged it for 2,300 years.

quiz.question: What evidence of violence was found on the Kyrenia ship?
options: Burned timber from a fire attack
Spearheads embedded in the hull and scattered cargo suggesting a pirate attack
Sword marks on the mast from a boarding party

details.summary: The Kyrenia ship, discovered off Cyprus in 1965, is a 4th-century BCE Greek merchant vessel preserved with its cargo of wine amphorae and almonds. It is the most completely preserved ancient Greek ship ever found, and a full-scale sailing replica proved it was seaworthy and efficient.
details.whyItMatters: The Kyrenia ship moved ancient shipbuilding from speculation to certainty. Its preserved hull revealed construction techniques described in no ancient text, and its sailing replica proved these designs were practical and efficient.
takeaways: The Kyrenia ship is the best-preserved ancient Greek vessel
Cargo included wine amphorae and almonds from the 4th century BCE
A sailing replica proved the ship design was seaworthy

faq.question: How was the Kyrenia ship built?
faq.answer: Using shell-first construction — planks were assembled first using mortise-and-tenon joints, then internal frames were added. This is opposite to the skeleton-first method used in later European shipbuilding. The technique produced strong, watertight hulls without modern fasteners.

faq.question: What happened to the Kyrenia ship replica?
faq.answer: Named Kyrenia II, the replica was built using ancient techniques and sailed the Mediterranean successfully. It proved the original design could handle open-sea conditions, achieve reasonable speeds, and carry substantial cargo — validating archaeological reconstruction through experimental method.
